t: The Taíno lived in villages of large round houses around a central plaza, farmed cassava in heaped mounds and were ruled by caciques, whose office usually passed through the female line.
Their religion centred on zemís, spirits and ancestors given form in carved wood, stone, shell and cotton, and honoured with cohoba snuff, songs and ceremonies.
Spanish conquest after 1492 brought forced labour, war and epidemics that killed most Taíno within decades, yet Taíno descent, customs and identity survive in the Caribbean today.
dyk: The English words barbecue, hammock, canoe, tobacco, savanna and hurricane all come from Taíno words: barbacoa, hamaca, kanoa, tabaco, sabana and juracán.
ev: Pottery-making farmers of the Ceramic Age, ancestors of the Taíno, enter the Caribbean from north-eastern South America
A woman later studied as an “ancient Taíno” lives in the Bahamas; her genome was mapped in 2018
Christopher Columbus lands in the Bahamas, on the island the Taíno called Guanahaní
On his second voyage Columbus begins to demand tribute in gold and cotton from the Taíno of Hispaniola
Caciques of Puerto Rico, among them Agüeybaná II, rise against the Spanish, while Antonio de Montesinos denounces the enslavement of the islanders
The cacique Hatuey, who had fled from Hispaniola to Cuba to unite its peoples, is burned at the stake
Enriquillo leads more than 3,000 Taíno in a successful rebellion on Hispaniola and wins land and a royal charter
9,399 people in Puerto Rico identify as Taíno in the United States census

f.homeland: The Lucayan Archipelago (the Bahamas), Cuba, Jamaica, Hispaniola (Haiti and the Dominican Republic) and Puerto Rico, east to Guadeloupe; ceremonial grounds such as Tibes in Puerto Rico.
f.period: Ceramic Age ancestors entered the Caribbean c. 2,500 years ago; Taíno chiefdoms met the Spanish in 1492; Spanish documents called them extinct by 1550, but their descendants and revival communities live on today.
f.known: chiefdoms (cacicazgos) ruled by caciques; matrilineal succession; worship of zemís; cassava grown in conuco mounds; the batey ball game; dugout canoes and cotton hammocks; words such as hammock, canoe, tobacco and hurricane
f.sources: Spanish chroniclers (Christopher Columbus, Ramón Pané, Bartolomé de las Casas, Peter Martyr d’Anghiera); excavated villages, ball courts, zemís and petroglyphs; DNA studies of ancient and living people; oral histories of descendant communities.
